title: Spare key
brief: Write an original short story for an adult literary magazine's issue on borrowed things. A person who cuts keys for a living is asked to identify an unlabelled key after a neighborhood shop closes for good. The story takes place over one ordinary afternoon. Make the request matter to at least two people whose interests differ. The setting, characters, action, structure and ending are yours to invent. Submit the finished story, without an explanation or author bio.

be7fcbaf52460c9e.text:
# Blanks

The key came in a margarine tub with eleven others, and the woman carrying the tub set it on my counter the way you set down something you've been asked to carry for somebody else.

"These are from Okafor's," she said. "The dry cleaner. You'll have seen it's shut."

I had. The paper went up in the window in September, and by the end of October the rail that used to carry everybody's coats round the ceiling had been taken down and sold. My booth is in the arcade across the road, between the phone repair man and a unit that has been four different nail bars. I'd looked at Okafor's window for nineteen years. I'd had my one suit cleaned there twice, for funerals.

"I'm Ngozi," she said. "His daughter. I'm clearing the place. The landlord wants the keys back Friday, all of them, and I don't know which are his."

"Which are the landlord's."

"Which are anybody's." She tipped the tub slightly so I could see. "Dad's in Leicester with my brother now. He's not good on the phone. He says they're all important."

I took them out one at a time and laid them on the rubber mat. It isn't difficult, most of it. A key tells you what it is if you've handled enough of them. Two were for the shop's front door, a five-lever mortice, one original and one copy, and the copy was mine. I know my own cutting like handwriting. A cylinder key for the shutter padlock. A little flat one for a till. Two window keys, a meter cupboard key, the triangular kind the gas people use. A car key for a Vauxhall that I would bet had been scrap for a decade.

"That's the back door," I said, moving a rim cylinder key to the left. "Those go to the landlord. This lot's yours to bin or keep. He'll not want a till key."

She was writing it down on the back of an envelope, which I liked. Then I picked up the last one.

It was a Yale type, brass, worn pale along the shoulder where a thumb goes. No tag, no tape, no dab of nail varnish. But it was a copy, and it was one of mine. I use a particular blank for that profile, from a supplier in Walsall, with a round bow where most have a clover. And I deburr on the wheel in one pass, upward, which leaves a faint slant at the tip. I've been told it's a bad habit.

"This one isn't the shop's," I said.

"What is it, then?"

"Somebody's front door. A house or a flat."

"Dad's house?"

"Have you got his house key on you?"

She had. She put it beside the other and even she could see it: different cuts altogether, a high first peak where the unlabelled one ran low.

"So whose is it?"

I should have said I couldn't tell. It was nearly true. But I turned it over, and on the bow, in the place where the blank has its flat, somebody had scratched a small cross with a pin. I do that. I do it when I'm cutting a set for one customer and they want to know which is which. One plain, one crossed.

And I remembered the set, because it's the only time anyone has asked me to cut a key they were plainly embarrassed to be cutting. A tall woman, sixtyish, in the green tabard of the school kitchen. Four or five years back. She'd wanted one spare, then changed her mind while I was at the machine and wanted two, and when I asked did she want them marked she said, *Mark the one that's not for me.*

"I'd have to look into it," I said.

Ngozi put her pen down. "Look into it how? Is there a register?"

"No. There's me."

"Because if it's a customer's key," she said, "if somebody left it with him, I need to know. I've had three people come to the door about a duvet and a wedding dress. I've got a box of unclaimed things I'm legally supposed to hold for I don't know how long. I don't want a key in that box. I want to hand over a clean shop on Friday and get his deposit back, which is two months' rent, which he needs." She said it without heat. She had a lanyard round her neck from some office, turned so the photo faced her chest. She'd come in her lunch hour, I thought, and her lunch hour had been over a while.

"Leave it with me till five," I said. "The others you can take."

She looked at the key and then at me. "It's only a key."

"It's a key to where somebody lives."

She left it. She took the tub.

---

The woman in the green tabard was called Maureen Pask, and I knew that not from the cutting but from the arcade, the way you know everybody eventually. She came through on Thursdays with a wheeled bag. She lived in the maisonettes on Carrow Street, behind the dry cleaner's, close enough that from her kitchen she would have seen the steam coming out of his back vent.

I didn't have her number. I had her Thursday, and it was Thursday.

Before she came, I had Dennis. Dennis is the landlord's man, not the landlord. The landlord is a company with a name like a mattress. Dennis does the keys and the meter readings for nine units on the parade, and he brings me their work, which over a year is a tenth of my takings. He came at two for some padlocks I'd keyed alike and saw the brass on the mat.

"That one of Okafor's?"

"His daughter was in."

"She's supposed to be bringing those to me." He picked it up. Dennis has small, clean hands and he holds things as if pricing them. "What's this for?"

"Not the shop."

"You sure? Because there's a flat above. Was let separately, years back, then he had it for storage. There's a door on the side passage. I've got no key for that door on my board and I've had to tell the office that, and they've told me that if there's no full set Friday they're charging a lock change to the deposit. All locks. Three hundred and forty."

"It's not that door either. That's a mortice. I fitted it."

"You'd swear to that."

"I'd show you. Go and look at the door."

He put the key down, not on the mat but on the counter nearer himself. "All I'm saying is, if it came out of that shop, it's part of what comes back to us. Then it's on my board and it's not my problem what it opens. She hands me twelve keys, I tick twelve, he gets his money. She hands me eleven and a story, I've got to write the story down." He paid for the padlocks. "I'm trying to do her a favour, as it goes."

He was, by his lights. A key on Dennis's board sits on Dennis's board until the building falls down. Nobody would ever try it in a door. It would also, forever, be a key to Maureen Pask's home hanging in an office she'd never heard of, under the wrong label.

"She's back at five," I said.

"Then I'll be back at five."

---

Maureen came through at twenty to four with the wheeled bag. I'd been watching for the tabard, but of course she'd retired; she was in a blue anorak, and I nearly missed her.

"Mrs Pask."

She came over. She looked at the machine and the boards of blanks behind me, the hundreds of them hanging uncut, and not at the mat.

"I've had the keys in from Okafor's," I said. "There's one I think I cut for you."

She looked then. She didn't pick it up.

"He kept it," she said.

"It was in a tub with the shop keys."

"A tub." She almost laughed. "That'd be right. He had a tub for everything. Buttons out of pockets. He'd give you your buttons back in a little bag." She put one finger on the key and moved it a quarter inch. "I had a fall. That's all it was to start with. On the stairs, and I lay there from tea-time till the milk. After that my sister said give somebody a key, and I thought, who's there six days a week, seven till seven, right out the back? So I took him one. I said, if my kitchen blind's not up by nine, come and knock, and if I don't answer, come in."

"And did he?"

"He knocked twice in five years. Once I'd gone to Skegness and not told him." She did laugh then. "He was that cross. Stood on my step on the Monday in his apron and told me off."

"It's yours to take," I said. "I only wanted to be sure whose it was."

"What does the daughter want with it?"

"She wants to know it's not the landlord's. The landlord's man wants it to be the landlord's. Makes his count right."

"Does it cost her if it's not?"

"It might cost her an argument."

Maureen thought about that. She took her purse out of the wheeled bag and her own keys out of the purse, and held her door key against the one on the mat, plain bow by crossed bow, the same teeth. Hers was the bright one. His had gone pale.

"He never said he was going," she said. "I saw the paper in the window same as everybody. I thought, he'll come round with it. Then I thought, he's forgotten he's got it. I didn't like either." She put her own keys away. "Nobody's had my blind to look at since September. I've been putting it up anyway. Daft."

"You could give it to somebody else."

"I could." She didn't take it. "You hang on to it till the girl comes. I want her to have it from me. I want her to know what he did with it."

---

At five there were three of them at a counter built for one. Dennis had his board list. Ngozi still had her coat on and the envelope.

"It's this lady's front door," I said. "I cut it. That's my mark."

"Lent," Maureen said. "Not left. There's a difference, for your box."

Ngozi looked at her. "He had a key to your house?"

"He had the looking-out of my kitchen blind." And she told it again, shorter, with Skegness in. Ngozi listened with her mouth slightly open, and at the apron on the doorstep she put her hand over it.

"He never said a word."

"No, well. I asked him not to. I didn't want it round the parade that I'd been on the stairs all night."

Dennis cleared his throat. "I've still got twelve down from the inventory. Okafor signed for twelve in 2009."

"Then your twelfth's the Vauxhall," I said. "Or I'll cut you something for the hook."

He looked at me to see if I meant it. I took a blank off the board, a Walsall one, round bow, and held it out to him uncut. He didn't take it. But he wrote something on his list, a long something, and when he'd finished he said, "Eleven and a note," to Ngozi, and that he'd see her Friday, and went.

Maureen picked up the key at last. She held it out across the counter, the crossed bow first.

"You're in Leicester, are you?"

"No," Ngozi said. "I'm on Pell Road. I'm ten minutes."

"That's no good for a blind."

"No."

"Still," Maureen said, and kept her hand where it was.

Ngozi took the key. She put it on her own ring, working it round the split steel with her thumbnail, between her office fob and her father's house key.

I pulled the shutter half down after them. The blank was still in my hand, and I hung it back on its hook.

d2ea4a3d71012b9a.text:
The Working Copy

At a quarter past one, a boy came in for a copy of a front-door key and paid Sonia in fifty-cent pieces. He counted them out in stacks of four. His mother had begun work at the hospital and from now on he would be letting himself in.

“Try it while she’s home,” Sonia said.

“She won’t be home. That’s why I need it.”

He put the key on a blue shoelace and went out swinging it, already careless of the responsibility he had wanted her to understand.

Across the street, two men were taking the name off Bell’s Office Supply. The B came away whole. Each of the smaller letters broke at least once. Sonia had been looking at that sign from behind her counter for twenty-three years, and by the time the boy reached the corner she could no longer have said whether the apostrophe had been painted or made of metal.

June Bell came in holding a key on her flat palm.

“What does this open?”

It was a little brass key, dark at the shoulder, with a round head and a hole worn oval. Sonia picked it up.

“Some kind of cabinet, probably.”

“Could you come over and tell me which?”

“Is the question which cabinet, or what’s in it?”

“I know what’s in it. I need you to tell Walter it’s ours.”

Through the glass Sonia could see Walter Pike sitting on a red swivel chair on the pavement. He had worked for June’s father long enough to have acquired the settled bearing of a proprietor, though never the pay. Behind him stood a grey steel cabinet about the height of a washing machine.

“My father left everything in the shop to me,” June said. “Walter says I can have the cabinet but the contents belong to other people. He’s refusing to get off the chair.”

“He’d have to be sitting on the cabinet for that to work.”

“He has a bad hip. Come across, would you?”

Sonia turned her sign to BACK SHORTLY. Her lunch, still in its paper, went in the drawer she kept for customers’ umbrellas. The shop had no sensible place to put a sandwich, but plenty of places to put keys.

The cabinet had twelve shallow drawers and a single lock at the top. She recognised the key before she tried it. For years Bell’s had sent people over for duplicates. A copy for the new Saturday girl, a copy for the porter, a copy once for a man who came in with a live pigeon held to his chest. She remembered the bird because he had set it on the counter to get his money out and it had stayed exactly where he put it, as if terrible terms had been agreed upon elsewhere.

The key turned. Sonia pulled open the top drawer. Inside stood a row of khaki envelopes with names on them.

“Thank you,” June said.

“That’s the cabinet it fits,” Sonia said.

“And whose key was it?”

“Whoever had it, I suppose.”

Walter rolled his chair closer by hauling on the doorframe. “Show her one.”

June took out an envelope. From it she drew a photograph of four women on a beach. Three were sitting on a blanket, the fourth bending down to ease off a shoe. The fourth woman’s long hair hung over her face and almost reached the sand.

“People brought things in to have them copied,” June said. “Dad kept whatever they didn’t collect. I’ve rung everybody I could trace. The historical society will take the rest provided I sign for them. They’re coming at four.”

“She means sign them over,” Walter said.

“They have proper storage. They’ll put the pictures on their website and somebody might recognise a grandmother.”

“Somebody might recognise another man’s wife.”

“Walter has been enjoying that possibility since breakfast.”

He looked at the photograph. “Mrs Vacca,” he said, touching the bent woman’s bare ankle.

“You can’t even see her face,” June said.

“Her husband took the picture. He was particular about having all of her in the copy. She’d died by then.”

June put the photograph away. The men with the sign had gone to lunch, leaving the pavement gritty with plaster. A bus pulled in, let nobody off and took nobody on. Sonia could have crossed back to her sandwich. Instead she pulled out the second drawer.

The first envelope said MORRIS, E. That was her mother.

Inside lay a sheet of lined paper folded in thirds. At the top, her mother had written the address of the house where Sonia grew up. Beneath it were the words *Dear Sir, I am asking for the return of my deposit.* She knew the letter. Her mother had borrowed forty dollars from her at a time when Sonia, who was seventeen, was saving for a green leather jacket. The landlord had kept the damage deposit on their old flat, and until the money came back, her mother said, there would be forty dollars too little in the world.

Sonia had never got the jacket. She had not thought of it in years and could see now every silver tooth of the zip.

“Can I have this?” she asked.

“Of course,” June said. “Take the envelope too.”

Walter reached out. “Let me see the back.”

Sonia turned the page. It was blank.

“Hold it slant.”

There was a shallow dent in the paper at the bottom, the length of somebody’s thumbnail.

“That’s how he picked them up,” Walter said.

“Who?”

“Your dad,” he said to June. “Off the glass. His nail left that little moon. The ones with the dent went back to the customer.”

“Well, this one evidently didn’t.”

Walter took the letter and laid it on the cabinet. He rubbed his finger across the address and held it up for them. A little black dust had come away on the whorls.

“It’s a copy,” he said. “Even the dent’s a picture of a dent. We used to leave a sheet of grey card on top so the thin places wouldn’t come out black. Your father kept a copy of everything for a while. In case there was a complaint.”

June slit the next envelope with the key. Two small boys stood squarely in front of a car. She turned it over. The back was plain white.

“Photographic paper has a maker’s mark,” Walter said. “Usually.”

“You said these belonged to people.”

“I said the things in here weren’t ours to give away.”

She sat down on the doorstep. Someone had chalked the price of printer cartridges on the stone beside her left shoe. “Did he ask?”

Walter worked his chair back and forth over a loose bit of plaster until it was powder. “In those days it took a couple of goes to get a decent likeness. If you had one left over, you kept it. Nobody wanted to stand there and watch you put their kid in the bin.”

“That wasn’t my question.”

“I heard you, June.”

Sonia read the rest of her mother’s letter. There was a list of the things the landlord had claimed were damaged. A curtain track. A white enamel basin. Under that, in the careful upright hand her mother used with people who had the power to disappoint her, a sentence Sonia had never heard her say. *My daughter and I lived quietly in your house and took pleasure in it.*

How her mother would have hated having that read out in a room. Even this much, on a pavement, felt like something she ought to ask about. She folded it into quarters, then opened it and folded it again along the lines her mother had made.

“I rang your shop,” June said to Walter. “When Dad was in hospital. He wanted to talk to you about this cabinet.”

Walter’s shop was a counter at the Sunday market where he sold old postcards from revolving racks. Sonia had once bought a view of the municipal baths from him and sent it to her brother in Perth.

“I went in,” he said.

“You never told me.”

“He wanted me to take the top two drawers. Said there were some street scenes I could make a bit on.”

“And you came to tell me I shouldn’t give them away?”

“I came for my drawers. Then you told me what you were planning for the rest.”

Sonia’s shop door rattled across the street. The boy with the blue shoelace had come back. She raised her arm and he saw her. He held up the key.

“Didn’t work?” she called.

He shook his head. A woman in hospital greens stood beside him, holding a bicycle. Sonia went over and let them in. While she checked the cut, the boy explained that the key went in and wouldn’t turn. His mother took off her glasses and cleaned them on her sleeve. There was a small blue bruise where the bridge rested on her nose.

“You have to pull the door toward you,” she said at last.

“You never told me that.”

“I thought you’d seen me do it.”

“I’m always behind you.”

Sonia took a light burr off the key. “Try it with the door open first. Then shut it and try what your mum says.”

They went out together, the boy walking the bicycle so his mother could eat a pear. Sonia retrieved her sandwich. By then it was three o’clock. Across the road Walter and June were going through the drawers, laying envelopes in separate piles. She ate standing up. The sandwich was cheese and mustard, cut so badly on the diagonal that one half was nearly a whole sandwich and the other was a corner you might give a dog.

At ten to four June brought the little key back.

“We’ve put aside the ones we’re sure are originals,” she said. “Walter’s going to help me take them round. I told the society they can have the shop ledgers and the Christmas window photographs. They sounded quite pleased.”

“What about the copies?”

“Dad bought a shredder for the accountants next door in 1998. They paid for it but never could get it through their door. I’ve spent twenty-eight years telling him to get rid of it.”

Across the street Walter was feeding handfuls into a machine on wheels. It took a while on photographs. He stood with both hands resting on top of it as though waiting for a calf to drink.

“And his street scenes?” Sonia asked.

“He’s keeping the ones Dad took himself. There’s a lovely one of your place before you came. Used to be a shop that sold nothing but eggs. Did you know that?”

Sonia hadn’t known.

“Have you got a minute to make another of these?” June asked. “He’ll need to come and go till we’re finished.”

Sonia found a blank and set the two keys in the jaws of the machine. June leaned against the counter, looking through the window at the man across the road, who had taken off his jacket. There was a patch of fresh pink skin on his elbow. At some point that afternoon he must have scraped it. Sonia wondered which of them had found him a plaster and why it had come off.

She brushed the new key clean. June took it, then took the old one too, a key in each hand. For a moment she considered them. She put the bright one in her pocket.

At half past four, alone again, Sonia unfolded her mother’s letter and laid it on the counter. She tried to bring the old flat back entire. The front room came easily, then the passage and the narrow ledge where the telephone stood. For the kitchen she had only a square of sunlight on some brown tiles and the smell of a gas ring just turned off. She had forgotten living quietly there. It was a relief to have somebody’s word for it.

She put the letter back in its envelope. On the front, below her mother’s name, she wrote her own.

8315f45d85f57eb3.text:
At one fifteen, Mrs. Vale brought in a key wrapped in a receipt from the shop that had closed next door. The receipt was for two tins of tomatoes and a birthday candle in the shape of a seven. My father had sold that candle to somebody on his last Saturday in business. He had priced it at twenty cents, which was less than the tax on most things I sold.

“Tell me what it opens,” Mrs. Vale said.

I laid it on the counter. It was a small brass key with three cuts and a square head. Someone had ground the manufacturer’s name off the head, leaving a shallow dish in the metal.

“Where was it?”

“In the shop.”

“I got that far.”

“Under the scale. He told me to look under the scale.”

My father had kept a balance scale on the counter long after he stopped selling anything by weight. Children put their elbows on one pan and tried to lift a pound of iron with the other. During the clearance that morning I had sold it for twelve dollars to a man who said his wife would kill him. Mrs. Vale must have come in after I went back to my own shop. The door between the two was still unlocked.

“What else did he tell you?”

“That if I ever needed to get in, that was where the key would be.”

“Get in where?”

She took off her glasses and looked at me. Her glasses made her eyes look smaller, and without them she had the startled appearance of a person receiving news.

“I thought you’d know.”

My father was at my sister’s for the week, learning how to use a shower with a glass door. At noon he had called to ask whether I’d found a buyer for the scale. I could have called him back. I put the key on the rubber mat where I set things I meant to examine.

“What do you need to get into?”

“I need my rent money,” she said.

Mrs. Vale lived above the shop. For thirty years she had taken in alterations, using a bell on a string to summon customers from the pavement. Since the funeral parlor had started buying its suits online, she mostly hemmed trousers for boys with interviews. I knew because she sent them to me for shoe polish and I sent them back upstairs so she could tell them to take the polish off the welt.

She had given my father nine hundred dollars to hold. In her account, he offered after the plumbers came in March. They had left her kitchen door open and a man she didn’t know had stood there eating a pear. She had gone downstairs with her money that same evening. Each month she took some out and put some in. Her new landlord wanted the rent by five.

“Did he give you a receipt?”

“He used to count it in front of me.”

My brother Dan came through the connecting door holding a shelf bracket. He had bought the building from our father two years earlier, and that morning he had let us have the clearance without charging for another day. He meant to be generous about it. His new tenant was coming at four to take measurements for a dog wash.

“Whose rent?” he asked.

“Mine,” said Mrs. Vale.

Dan set the bracket on the mat, knocking the key to the floor. He went down on both knees to find it. The floor on my side was black rubber, and customers were always telling me how good it must be for my back.

When he stood up he held the key by the point.

“I’ve been looking for this,” he said.

He took it through to the shop. Mrs. Vale and I followed. With the shelves down you could see that my father had painted around them three times, so that the walls carried bands of cream, yellow and a blue so faint it looked like light coming through the plaster.

Dan crouched beside the old register. It sat on a stand with a steel cabinet underneath, which he planned to roll out onto the pavement. He put the key in the cabinet lock. It went all the way in. He tried turning it twice, with increasing faith.

“Let me,” I said.

He handed it over. I could feel one pin lift and catch. It was the right kind of blank. Somebody could have bought a dozen of them and cut keys for half the cabinets in the neighborhood.

“I can open this,” I said. “It’ll take a minute.”

Dan looked at Mrs. Vale. “What’s in it is Dad’s.”

“Some of what’s Dad’s is mine,” she said.

“I’ll ask him.”

He called from where he stood. We heard my sister answer and tell him that Dad had gone to sleep in the car on the way back from the pharmacy, and that she had left him there with the window down. Dan asked her to go wake him. She said she’d been out twice to check the shade and she was eating her lunch.

“Call back at three,” she said. “He’ll have to pee by then.”

Mrs. Vale sat down on the little wooden step my father had used to reach the cigarettes. She had a flat brown purse with what looked like sugar down one seam. She pinched a little of it out and tasted it. Then she pinched out some more and offered it to me.

“Peppermint,” she said.

Dan went outside to look for the dolly he had lent the man who bought the scale. I went back to my side and cut two copies of an apartment key for a woman whose daughter was coming home. She tried to decide between a blue cap and a red one, finally taking both. I never asked people whether their children were coming home for good. They tended to tell me in the pause while I brushed the filings off the keys. This woman watched me brush and said she had made up the bed.

At two I turned the sign to BACK IN TEN and brought my picks through. Mrs. Vale was standing at the counter, examining the round black circle where the scale had been.

“He did tell me where,” she said. “He said, ‘Put it with the money.’ I told him that was no place to put a key, and he said, ‘All right, the scale.’ So I knew if I had the key I’d be able to find the money.”

I opened the steel cabinet. It held a case of paper bags, three pink rolls of register tape and two white china cups. The cups had been upside down on their saucers long enough to leave clean rings. Inside one cup were the dead batteries my father used to give customers when they asked how big a battery they needed.

Mrs. Vale turned the other cup over. It was the kind that used to come free with a pound of coffee. She looked at its underside for a long time, and then set it back where it had been.

Dan returned with the dolly and a sandwich in a paper sleeve. He broke the sandwich in half, offered me the smaller half and gave the larger one to Mrs. Vale. She took it, picked out the peppers and handed them back to him.

“Could he have meant the money upstairs?” Dan asked.

Mrs. Vale stopped chewing.

“I mean his own money,” he said. “When Dad first opened, he used to go upstairs to make change. Mom kept a cashbox.”

“You’ve been in my apartment?” she asked.

“When I was nine.”

By then I knew the box he meant. I could remember my mother levering the tray up from one corner because she’d fill the space underneath with notes until the tray buckled. There was a keyhole just below the handle. The box itself had been green, though from a height it looked gray, like the money in it.

Mrs. Vale folded the sleeve around the uneaten end of her sandwich. “I have a green box,” she said. “Your mother lent it to me.”

She went up to get it. I heard the bell on her string ring once, as it did whenever she opened the door wide enough to admit herself sideways with both hands full. Dan wheeled the cabinet to the curb. A scrap of adhesive tape had stuck to the bottom. He peeled it off and carried it to my wastebasket, and for some reason I remembered him at nine, visiting every room of the house with a bowl of plum pits while my mother told him to put them in the garbage. He wanted somebody to see how many plums he’d eaten.

Mrs. Vale came down with the box wrapped in a dress. She laid it on the counter and put the dress over her arm. The box was greener than I remembered, especially around the handle, where the enamel was worn to a pale jade. There were scratches all around the keyhole.

“I tried my nail scissors,” she said. “Years ago.”

“What did Mom lend it to you for?” Dan asked.

“I needed something heavy to keep the pattern paper flat. She brought it up and then she couldn’t find the key. I told her it was doing its job.”

The key entered cleanly. I turned it a quarter turn and the bolt slid back. All three of us heard it. I left the lid down and pushed the box across to Mrs. Vale.

She had to put the dress down to open it. There was no tray inside. On the bottom lay a white bank envelope and, beside it, a loose brass handle from a drawer. Mrs. Vale pulled the envelope out and dipped her fingers in. She counted nine hundred dollars onto the counter, laying each hundred partly over the last. Some were made up of twenties. One was made up of fives.

Dan picked up the brass handle. “From the bread drawer,” he said.

“What bread drawer?” I asked.

“We had one.” He turned the handle over and ran his thumb across the two small threaded holes. “I remember the bread.”

At three the phone rang. It was my father, awake and delighted at having slept. He said my sister’s car was the first car in which he could get comfortable without moving the seat. Then he asked if Mrs. Vale had come in.

“She’s here,” I said. “We opened the box.”

He was quiet a little while. “Did she bring it down?”

“Yes.”

“I went up while she was at the dentist. I had her spare, for the pipes. I couldn’t think where else to put it once the shop was going.”

I watched Mrs. Vale gather the notes, trying to get all the edges even enough to go back in the envelope. She pushed too hard, and one of the fives folded. I thought about the man with the pear, whether he’d picked it up in her kitchen or come in eating it. I told my father I’d call him later.

“He used your spare to put it there,” I said.

Mrs. Vale finished putting away the fives. “I’d like my spare, too.”

I found it on the board next door, hanging from a nail with a paper tag giving her name and the best hour to catch her in. On the back my father had written *ring twice*. I brought it to her with the little brass key. She put her spare in the purse and slid the box toward Dan.

“Take it,” she said. “I’ve got an iron I can use.”

Dan rested a hand on the lid. Then he opened it and set the bread drawer handle inside. He asked me to cut a copy of the little key. He paid for it, even though he had heard me tell people all morning that I wasn’t charging for anything that had to do with the shop closing.

I cut the copy, and from the doorway he watched me work. Next door there was a knock, three brisk raps on a door that stood open. The woman from the dog wash called his name. He left the box on the counter between us and went to meet her with the bright new key in his hand.

Mrs. Vale picked up her dress. It was a man’s striped shirt with the sides opened, I saw now, and a skirt of the same material pinned to it. She folded it once over her forearm. I held out the old key, thinking she might like to keep it after all. She took it and fitted it into the lock. When she pressed the lid down, it lifted a little against her palm, and she had to press harder to turn the key. Then she set the key beside the box, where Dan could see it when he came back, and went upstairs to pay him.
